figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Pass rate on SWE-bench. (a) Linear ReAct vs. MCTS on SWE-bench Lite (Antoniades et al., 2025). (b) Base vs. RL-trained on SWE-bench Verified (Wei et al., 2025; Golubev et al., 2025; Agentica and Together AI, 2025).
figures.headline: Tree search raises pass rate on SWE-bench Lite over single linear generation.
citing_sentences: Search lifts solve rates over single linear generation (Fig.​ 1).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Design Overview. DeltaBox uses diff-based checkpoint/restore (deltaCheckpoint and deltaRestore) to enable millisecond-level checkpoint/rollback. The agent worker runs inside the sandbox, so every step is C/R-protected and can be rolled back promptly when needed.
figures.headline: Diff-based checkpoint and restore let every agent step be rolled back promptly inside the sandbox.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: The DeltaBox architecture. The StateManager coordinates DeltaFS (Layer 2, filesystem state) and DeltaCR (Layer 3, process state). Base storage (Layer 1) is an XFS volume with reflink, providing block-level CoW to eliminate file-size-proportional write amplification.
figures.headline: A layered architecture keeps each checkpoint a consistent filesystem and memory pair, coordinated by a StateManager.
citing_sentences: DeltaBox adopts a layered architecture (Fig.​ 3), coordinated by a StateManager that keeps every checkpoint a consistent, atomic (filesystem, memory) pair.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: DeltaFS architecture. (a) Traditional overlayfs will prepare an upper layer file system which is writable for apps, and maintain a lower layer file system which is read-only and basically includes everything in the sandbox image. (b) DeltaFS extends the idea to support dynamic overlay, i.e., when an agent finishes a step of task and needs to make a checkpoint, instead of duplicating all files, DeltaFS inserts a new writable layer above the existing one and freezes the existing writable layer into a read-only state, and all following updates are copy-on-write to the new upper layer. As a result, the checkpoint operation is simply a layer insert operation while a rollback is a set of layer remove operations.
figures.headline: Overlay layers are inserted at checkpoints and removed at rollback, so checkpointing costs one layer insert, not a full copy.
citing_sentences: The ioctl parses the new configuration, builds a layer array (one private mount clone per path), and performs an atomic swap: publishing the array via release-consistent stores, bumping the per-filesystem checkpoint_gen (red annotation in Fig.​ 4b), and invalidating stale dentry/inode caches.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: DeltaCR architecture. Checkpointing creates both a CRIU image and a frozen template. Restores use the template fast path on hit, or the CRIU image on miss; NPD keeps external I/O off the agent path.\agentcrcontroller checkpoints an active agent into a CRIU image and a frozen template pool. Restore uses the template pool on hit, the CRIU image on miss, and a sidecar for LLM network proxying.
figures.headline: Checkpoints produce both a process image and a frozen template, and restores use the template when it is still present.
citing_sentences: Fig.​ 5 summarizes these components and the two restore paths.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: End-to-end time for 30-iteration MCTS trajectories (Qwen3-Coder-30B) across four SWE-bench archetype groups, comparing DeltaBox against E2B (diff). Each system is normalized per group to its own LLM+action line (1.0$\times$ = LLM RTT + action work, i.e., the ideal end-to-end time if state management were free). For a fair comparison, we invoke E2B’s pause/resume primitives directly, measuring only the C/R substrate cost without control-plane overhead.
figures.headline: DeltaBox stays at 1.01–1.02 times ideal end-to-end time, while E2B (diff) reaches 1.30–1.93 times.
citing_sentences: (Table.​ 1 lists E2B’s documented full-VM pause, ${\sim}4$ s/GiB; the Table.​ 2 and Fig.​ 6 figures are this self-hosted incremental path, hence far lower.)
These savings become decisive once the LLM round-trip drops to seconds (Fig.​ 6).
Fig.​ 6 normalizes each instance’s end-to-end time to its own LLM+action latency: DeltaBox stays at 1.01–1.02$\times$, while E2B (diff) reaches 1.30–1.93$\times$.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: RL training fan-out characterisation. (a) End-to-end time to fork $N{\in}\{1,4,16,64\}$ memory-bearing children from one frozen source via each sandbox’s native fork/clone path (DeltaBox fork_n, CubeSandbox clone, E2B createSnapshot$+$create). The source touches 64 MiB and each child reads it back and verifies. E2B’s $N{=}64$ is 4 sequential 16-concurrency batches. (b) $T_{\text{gen}}$ (batched vLLM, $256{\to}512$ tok) and $T_{\text{train}}$ (Qwen2.5-7B LoRA-r16 fwd+bwd) for Qwen2.5-7B on 4 GPUs. (c) Expected sync GPU occupation $(T_{\text{gen}}{+}T_{\text{train}})/(\text{sandbox}{+}T_{\text{gen}}{+}T_{\text{train}})$ at $N{\in}\{16,64\}$ on Qwen2.5-7B, computed from (a) and (b).
figures.headline: DeltaBox forks memory-bearing children an order of magnitude or more faster than CubeSandbox and E2B across the measured range.
citing_sentences: RL training fan-out (Fig.​ 7b–c) additionally uses a single-node 4-GPU cluster (96 GB each).
Fig.​ 7(a) compares the three agent sandboxes that all deliver memory-bearing children through their native fork/clone path.
Across the measured range DeltaBox is an order of magnitude or more faster than both CubeSandbox and E2B (Fig.​ 7(a)).

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Per-event CoW fault absorption vs. post-restore idle window (50 swe-search MCTS restore events). Shaded band: p1–p99 idle range from 3,817 LLM-driven restore events under 4-GPU inference.
figures.headline: Copy-on-write fault cost after restore does not accumulate under the idle windows seen in realistic workloads.
citing_sentences: Fig.​ 8 verifies that lazy-CoW restore does not accumulate post-fork page-fault debt under realistic LLM idle windows.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Per-edit copy-up bytes (a) and physical I/O bytes (b) vs. edited-file size (log–log); real SWE-bench agent edits across three filesystem configurations, per-bin medians. Shaded band marks the typical agent edit range. ext4 and XFS-without-reflink coincide on (a): copy-up benefit comes entirely from reflink, not XFS.
figures.headline: With reflink, per-edit copy-up stays flat as file size grows, while ext4 and XFS without reflink grow linearly with size.
citing_sentences: Fig.​ 9(a) shows ext4 and XFS-without-reflink coinciding at every bin, both recopying the whole file on modification and growing linearly with size, while the reflink curve stays low and flat, widening the gap as files grow.

Fig.​ 9(b) shows that XFS’s lighter metadata bookkeeping dominates on small files (132 KB $\to$ 26 KB at 1–8 KB, with reflink adding little), while reflink’s block sharing dominates on large files (315 KB $\to$ 141 KB at 128–256 KB).

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Adaptive optimizations (87 MCTS runs, 9 SWE-bench repos). (a) Per-event checkpoint latency over 1,689 events: pure-read commands (LW, $n{=}1047$) skip the dump, FS-mutating (std, $n{=}642$) take it; 62.0% route to the LW peak. (b) End-of-trajectory CRIU dump storage (9 instances, 5 MB process): reachability-aware GC vs. retaining every checkpoint.
figures.headline: Reachability-aware garbage collection cuts end-of-trajectory dump storage by 46–63% compared with retaining every checkpoint.
citing_sentences: Since read-only steps dominate a typical trajectory, this lowers the in-VM snapshot-store footprint (10(a)), at the cost of replaying the action on the parent’s state at restore; we therefore enable LW only when snapshot memory, not restore latency, is the bottleneck.
Across nine SWE-bench MCTS trajectories replayed through real criu dump, it reduces end-of-trajectory dump storage by 46–63% versus retaining every checkpoint (10(b)).

abstract:
Emerging LLM-powered AI agent workloads, such as test-time tree search and reinforcement learning, require high-frequency state exploration, relying on rapid checkpoint and rollback (C/R) of the complete sandbox state, including files and process state. Existing mechanisms duplicate the entire state, causing hundreds of milliseconds to seconds of latency per C/R, which severely bottlenecks deep search and large-scale fan-outs.

This paper observes that consecutive sandbox states between checkpoints differ only slightly. Therefore, instead of full duplication, a sandbox should only duplicate the changes between consecutive checkpoints (Key Insight), yet the lack of OS support makes this hard to realize. We propose a new OS-level abstraction, DeltaState , that delivers change-based C/R for agents through two co-designed OS mechanisms. First, DeltaFS checkpoints file state by freezing the writable layer and inserting a new one, turning updates into copy-on-write and rollback into a layer switch. Second, DeltaCR rolls back by forking from a frozen template process, backed by a CRIU dump. Building on the two mechanisms, we present DeltaBox, an agent sandbox with millisecond-level C/R. On SWE-bench and RL micro-benchmarks, DeltaBox hides its checkpoint work ($\approx$10.83 ms) under inference and rolls back in $\approx$1.86 ms, letting agents explore more nodes under a fixed time budget.

sections.body: Agents that run tree search or reinforcement learning need to checkpoint and roll back the full sandbox state, including files and processes, at high frequency. The paper states that existing mechanisms duplicate the whole state, costing hundreds of milliseconds to seconds per checkpoint or rollback. Its key insight is that consecutive checkpoints differ only slightly, so only the changes between them should be duplicated. The proposed DeltaBox sandbox uses DeltaFS for filesystem state and DeltaCR for process state. The abstract reports checkpoint work of about 10.83 ms and rollback of about 1.86 ms on SWE-bench and reinforcement-learning micro-benchmarks.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Full-state duplication makes sandbox checkpoints cost hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, too slow for frequent agent rollback.

sections.body: Table 1 compares sandbox approaches on checkpoint latency, restore latency, write amplification, and support for filesystem state, process state, and arbitrary rollback. Filesystem-only tools discard process memory, while VM snapshots capture whole-VM memory at VM granularity. The table reports Firecracker VM snapshots at 200 ms–2 s for checkpoint and 120–700 ms for restore, and E2B at about 4 s per GiB of RAM for checkpoint. Best-of-N sampling and Monte Carlo tree search both need fast intermediate checkpoints. The section sets four requirements: millisecond-level coupled checkpoint and restore, write amplification proportional to actual changes, constant-time arbitrary rollback, and agent transparency.
sections.heading: Background and Motivation
sections.headline: Existing sandboxes either lack process-state rollback or snapshot whole virtual machines, so none covers both state dimensions efficiently.

sections.body: The StateManager issues a deltaCheckpoint during each language-model round-trip, persisting only the change in coupled memory and filesystem state for that step. A deltaRestore switches the overlay layer stack to the target in one operation. It then restores process memory by forking a warm template on a hit, or by loading the CRIU image chain on a miss. The base layer is an XFS volume with reflink. DeltaFS provides runtime layer reconfiguration, and DeltaCR provides process checkpoint and restore with an asynchronous dump and a template-creating fork. The stated SIGSTOP pause during checkpoint is about 11 ms, which the section says fits within seconds-scale inference latency.
sections.heading: System Overview
sections.headline: Each checkpoint stores only its per-step change, and rollback switches overlay layers then forks a warm template or restores a dump.

sections.body: DeltaFS extends overlayfs with an ioctl that swaps the layer stack without unmounting, and a lazy switch handles files left open across a checkpoint. Files modified after a checkpoint are copied up on XFS with reflink, so unchanged extents stay shared. DeltaCR keeps frozen template processes in a bounded pool. An evicted template falls back to the CRIU lazy-pages restore path. An async-warm thread pre-pays copy-on-write faults after each fork. A Network Proxy Daemon owns the LLM SDK clients and sockets, so templates stay forkable. The section states a limitation: DeltaBox does not currently support network I/O rollback, which may incur external side effects.
sections.heading: Detailed Design
sections.headline: The design swaps overlay layers at runtime and forks frozen templates, with a proxy keeping network sockets out of forked processes.

sections.body: DeltaFS is built on Linux 6.8 overlayfs, and the checkpoint ioctl adds about 565 lines of C across four files. The layer-array pointer is swapped atomically under a spinlock, and the old array is freed after an RCU grace period. DeltaCR is a userspace daemon of about 1200 lines of Python that orchestrates CRIU, the template pool, the async-warm thread, and the proxy daemon. The prototype runs inside Firecracker microVMs, and the section says the same optimizations apply to container or other VM sandboxes. A LangGraph checkpoint-saver adapter and explicit sandbox tool nodes provide framework integration. The host controller drives the guest daemon over virtio-vsock.
sections.heading: Implementation
sections.headline: The prototype adds about 565 lines of C to overlayfs and about 1200 lines of Python for the userspace daemon.

sections.body: Experiments run on a four-socket server with 96 physical cores and 760 GiB RAM. DeltaBox runs in a Firecracker microVM with 4 vCPUs and 8 GB RAM, on Qwen3-Coder-30B MCTS trajectories from four SWE-bench archetype groups. Baselines are replay with copytree, Firecracker diff with dm-snapshot, CRIU with copytree, and self-hosted E2B (diff). In Table 2, DeltaBox's weighted average checkpoint blocking is 10.83 ms and restore is 1.86 ms, against 899.7 ms restore for E2B (diff). Table 2 excludes the completion time of the asynchronous dump. End-to-end, state management takes 23–48% of time on E2B (diff) and 1–2% on DeltaBox.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: On SWE-bench tree-search trajectories, DeltaBox restores in 1.86 ms on weighted average, versus 899.7 ms for the incremental-snapshot baseline.

sections.body: Agent sandboxes such as Daytona, E2B, ZeroBoot, and Yan's fault-tolerant sandbox focus mainly on isolation and startup, with coarse-grained rollback. Serverless systems such as TrEnv-X and Spice optimize sandbox reuse and restore for single function invocations, which the section calls orthogonal to DeltaBox. Checkpoint tools such as CRIU, DMTCP, Firecracker, Btrfs, and ZFS provide building blocks but not coupled, fine-grained rollback for agents. Crab uses semantics-aware checkpoint granularity and is described as complementary to DeltaBox. A position paper frames agentic exploration as a systems problem that needs fast forking.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior agent sandboxes offer coarse rollback, and serverless restore work targets cold starts rather than repeated rollback within one task.

sections.body: The conclusion presents DeltaBox as an OS-level rollbackable sandbox for test-time tree search and reinforcement learning. It argues that subsequent agent states are highly similar, so diff-based checkpoint and restore replaces full state duplication. DeltaFS provides unmount-free overlay layer switching for filesystem checkpoint and restore. DeltaCR uses CRIU dumps and warm-template forking for memory checkpoint and restore. The conclusion does not add results beyond those reported in the evaluation.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Change-based checkpointing through DeltaFS and DeltaCR gives agent sandboxes millisecond-level rollback for search and reinforcement learning.
